Band theory (§1.9.1) considers two bands, formed when the energy levels of electrons in the closely spaced atoms of a solid interact — just as atomic orbitals interact to give molecular orbitals.

**Conduction band.** The highest energy band containing electrons. It is formed by interaction of the outermost energy levels of the closely spaced atoms, and it may be partially occupied or vacant. The electrons in the conduction band are mobile and delocalised over the entire solid, so they conduct electricity when an electrical potential is applied.

**Valence band.** The band having lower energy than the conduction band. Its electrons are **not** free to move, because they are tightly bound to their respective nuclei.

The energy difference between the two is the band gap; when it is too large for thermal energy to promote an electron across it, it is called the forbidden zone.

From §1.3.1, §1.3.3 and Table 1.1:

| Property | Ionic solids | Molecular solids |
|---|---|---|
| Constituent particles | cations and anions | molecules (or unbonded single atoms) |
| Interparticle forces | strong electrostatic (coulomb) attraction between oppositely charged ions | weak intermolecular forces — dipole-dipole, London dispersion, or hydrogen bonds |
| Hardness | hard and brittle | soft |
| Melting point | high (about \(600\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(3000\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) | low (about \(-272\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\) to \(400\,^\circ\mathrm{C}\)) |
| Electrical conductivity | nonconductors in the solid state, but good conductors when melted or dissolved in water | poor conductors of heat and electricity; good insulators |
| Examples | NaCl, \(\mathrm{K_2SO_4}\), \(\mathrm{CaF_2}\), KCl | ice, \(\mathrm{CO_2}\), \(\mathrm{CH_4}\), benzoic acid |

An fcc unit cell has particles at its eight corners and at the centre of each of its six faces (§1.5.1 iii).

**Corner particles.** Each corner of a cube is shared by 8 neighbouring cubes, so each corner particle contributes \(\tfrac{1}{8}\) to this cell:

contribution from corners \(= 8 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 1\) atom

**Face-centre particles.** Each face is shared between 2 neighbouring cubes, so each face-centre particle contributes \(\tfrac{1}{2}\):

contribution from faces \(= 6 \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 3\) atoms

**Total** \(= 1 + 3 = \mathbf{4}\) atoms per fcc unit cell.

**The first layer.** The spheres of the first layer are arranged in **square close packing** (§1.6.1 b i). One-dimensional rows of touching spheres are stacked over each other so that the spheres align both vertically and horizontally. Every sphere therefore touches four neighbouring spheres in its own layer, so the two-dimensional coordination number is 4, and joining the centres of those four closest neighbours gives a square.

**The successive layers.** Each following layer is placed so that its spheres lie **exactly above** the spheres of the layer below, with no offset (§1.6.1 c i). Since every layer is therefore identical to the first, all are labelled 'A' and the stacking pattern is described as **AAAA…** type.

This arrangement generates the simple cubic structure, whose unit cell is the primitive cubic unit cell. Each sphere then touches six neighbours — four in its own layer, one above and one below — so the coordination number in three dimensions is 6. Polonium is the only metal that crystallizes in this way.

**Step 1 — radius of the sphere.** In a simple cubic unit cell the particles are at the corners and touch each other along the edge, so

\(a = 2r\) and hence \(r = \dfrac{a}{2}\)

**Step 2 — volume of one sphere.**

\(V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi r^3 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi \left(\dfrac{a}{2}\right)^3 = \dfrac{\pi a^3}{6}\)

**Step 3 — total volume of particles.** A simple cubic unit cell contains only 1 particle, so the volume occupied by particles in the unit cell is \(\dfrac{\pi a^3}{6}\).

**Step 4 — packing efficiency.**

\(\text{Packing efficiency} = \dfrac{\text{volume occupied by particles in unit cell}}{\text{total volume of unit cell}} \times 100 = \dfrac{\pi a^3/6}{a^3} \times 100 = \dfrac{100\pi}{6}\)

\(= \dfrac{100 \times 3.142}{6} = \mathbf{52.36\%}\)

Thus 52.36 % of the total space in a simple cubic lattice is occupied by particles and 47.64 % is empty (void) space.

Section 1.10 (ii): **paramagnetic substances are those with unpaired electrons, which are weakly attracted by a magnetic field.**

The spinning of an unpaired electron gives rise to a magnetic moment, and it is this magnetic moment that causes the substance to be attracted. Such substances exhibit magnetism **only in the presence of an external magnetic field** — they lose their magnetism as soon as the field is removed. (Contrast ferromagnetic substances, which retain it.)

Examples given by the chapter: oxygen, \(\mathrm{Cu^{2\oplus}}\), \(\mathrm{Fe^{3\oplus}}\) and \(\mathrm{Cr^{3\oplus}}\).

A Schottky defect is a paired cation-anion vacancy: equal numbers of cations and anions are missing from their regular lattice sites. Section 1.8.1 (iii) lists two consequences:

1. **The density of the substance decreases.** Because ions are missing, the mass of the substance decreases, while the volume remains unchanged — so \(\rho = m/V\) falls.
2. **The electrical neutrality of the compound is preserved.** The number of missing cations is equal to the number of missing anions, so the positive and negative charge lost are equal and the crystal as a whole stays neutral.

The defect is found in ionic crystals such as NaCl, AgBr and KCl.

Count each kind of ion using the sharing rules of §1.5.1.

**\(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) ions at the corners.** Each corner of a cube is shared by 8 neighbouring cubes, so each corner ion contributes \(\tfrac{1}{8}\):

number of \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\) per unit cell \(= 8 \times \dfrac{1}{8} = 1\)

**\(\mathrm{Cs^{\oplus}}\) ion at the body centre.** A particle at the centre of the cube is not shared with any other cube, so it belongs entirely to this cell:

number of \(\mathrm{Cs^{\oplus}}\) per unit cell \(= 1\)

The unit cell therefore contains 1 \(\mathrm{Cs^{\oplus}}\) and 1 \(\mathrm{Cl^{\ominus}}\), that is **1 CsCl formula unit ("molecule") per unit cell**, consistent with the 1 : 1 formula CsCl.

For an fcc unit cell the corner particles touch the face-centre particle along the face diagonal, so \(4r = \sqrt{2}\,a\), giving (Table 1.3)

\(r = \dfrac{\sqrt{2}}{4}a = 0.3535\,a\)

With \(a = 495\ \mathrm{pm}\):

\(r = 0.3535 \times 495\ \mathrm{pm} = 174.98\ \mathrm{pm}\)

**The radius of the Cu atom is about \(175\ \mathrm{pm}\)** (that is, \(1.75 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}\)).

The derivation of §1.5.2, in five steps.

i. If the edge length of the cubic unit cell is \(a\), the volume of the unit cell is \(a^3\).

ii. Let the mass of one particle be \(m\) and let there be \(n\) particles per unit cell. Then

mass of unit cell \(= m \times n\)

iii. The density of the unit cell, which is the same as the density of the substance, is

\(\rho = \dfrac{\text{mass of unit cell}}{\text{volume of unit cell}} = \dfrac{m \times n}{a^3}\)

iv. The molar mass \(M\) is the mass of one particle times the number of particles per mole, so \(M = m \times N_A\), giving

\(m = \dfrac{M}{N_A}\)

v. Substituting for \(m\):

**\(\rho = \dfrac{n M}{a^3 N_A}\)**

This relates the density of a substance to the edge length of its unit cell. It contains five quantities — \(\rho\), \(n\), \(M\), \(a\) and \(N_A\) — so knowing any four of them allows the fifth to be calculated. (Note that \(\rho\) is inversely proportional to \(a^3\), so a small error in the edge length has a threefold effect on the density.)
